About: one Einstein mode in a heat bath — level spacing versus thermal budget

Source

Concept
One Einstein mode in a heat bath: an evenly spaced ladder En = n·ε (unbounded, no zero-point) in the canonical ensemble, with θ = ε/kB = 11.6045 K per meV.
Serves
NCERT / JEE thermal physics: equipartition, its quantum failure at low temperature, and the Dulong–Petit puzzle Einstein's 1907 ladder resolved.
Inquiry
Two commitments — what C/kB of one mode does when kBT drops well below ε, and what doubling ε does to the step on the C/kB chart.
Misconception
“Heat capacity is a fixed property of a substance — energy goes in smoothly at every temperature.”

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealThe C/kB chart and readout stay hidden until the freeze-out prediction is committed; the star control is predicted before it is dragged.
Misconception as a choice“Heat capacity is a fixed property” is a selectable option; its rebuttal appears only to the student who picks it.
Invariant made visibleC/kB depends on T/θ alone — on a log-T axis doubling ε translates the step rigidly, shape preserved to the last digit.
Fixed axes, honest scaleEnergy axis 0–120 meV, both temperature axes log 5–1500 K, C axis 0–1.1: nothing autoscales, so the slide is real and readable.
Operational quantitiesThe kBT bracket is drawn to the rungs' own energy scale, and every bar is a counted fraction of the ensemble.
Honest tailProbability above the drawn rungs is shown as a fading wedge with its percentage, never renormalized away.
Readout disciplineTwo readouts at load; C/kB and P₀ appear only at the step that asks the student to read them.
Toggleable formalismBoltzmann factors, ⟨E⟩, C and the scaling identity live behind ⚛︎ The Physics, so the sim works before or after the algebra.
Heat Capacity of One Einstein Mode
✦Ask Euler
One Einstein mode in a heat bath — the ladder, the kBT ruler, and where the step stands

Guided Inquiry

1 · The ladder and the budget

Let’s get to know the ladder. Every system in this large ensemble climbs the same one, rungs ε = 10 meV apart. The bars give the fraction of systems on each rung. The bracket beside them is the thermal budget kBT, drawn to the same energy scale. How does the bracket compare with the first gap?

2 · Predict: cool to θ/10

Time for a prediction. Suppose you cool from 40 K to 11.6 K — one tenth of θ. What do you think this mode’s heat capacity C/kB would do?

3 · Cool it and watch

Let’s try it. A new chart beside the ladder now plots C/kB against temperature, with a readout to match. Drag T down toward 12 K and watch three things: the bars spill onto the ground rung, the kBT bracket shrink under the first gap, and the marker walk down the step.

4 · Frozen out, not gone

How did your prediction do? Check it against the C/kB and P₀ readouts: almost every system now sits on the ground rung and C has collapsed far below kB. The mode hasn’t vanished — it’s frozen out, waiting for a budget that can buy a rung.

5 · Predict: double the spacing

Let’s move somewhere more interesting. Warm T until the C/kB readout reads 0.500 — the marker then sits exactly halfway up the step. Now suppose you double ε from 10 to 20 meV. What do you think happens to the step?

6 · Drag the spacing

Let’s find out. A second chart has appeared above C: average energy ⟨E⟩ per system versus T — its knee marks where the budget starts affording rungs. Now drag ε slowly from 10 to 20 meV. Watch the rungs spread against the unchanged bracket while the step below and the knee above slide together — and keep an eye on the parked marker as it gets left behind.

7 · Same shape, new address

So what moved? The half-step marker on the lower chart sits at T = 0.335 θ — read where it moved to. The parked marker fell off the step into freeze-out. Nothing about the shape changed — only where it stands, because C depends on T/θ alone.

8 · Why diamond broke Dulong–Petit

Now for a famous real-world puzzle. At 300 K the ruler reads kBT ≈ 25.8 meV, yet this widest ladder still delivers C/kB ≈ 0.82 — check the readout. Diamond’s stiffest vibrations sit near 165 meV, about four times this slider’s widest gap. What do you think that does to C at room temperature?

The Physics

Heat capacity steps · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A vibration in a solid can take in energy only in whole steps of size ε. This sim sets that step against the thermal energy kBT and shows what the comparison does to the mode's heat capacity, the heat it can absorb per kelvin.

What you'll learn

  • How a ladder of equally spaced levels fills at a given temperature.
  • How one mode's heat capacity depends on kBT compared with ε.
  • How the heat-capacity curve moves when ε changes.
  • How the same comparison applies to real solids and gases.
One mode: rungs at En = nε, bars for the fraction of systems on each rung, and the thermal energy kBT on the same scale.

What's on screen

  • Rungs (blue): levels n = 0 to 9 on a fixed 0–120 meV scale.
  • Bars (orange): the fraction of systems on each rung. The wedge gives the percentage above rung 9.
  • kBT bracket (amber): the thermal energy, on the same scale as the rungs.
  • ⟨E⟩ chart (teal): average energy against T, on a log axis.
  • C/kB chart (orange): heat capacity against T, with an amber half-step marker. Dots mark the current T.
  • Readouts: θ = ε/kB, kBT, C/kB and P₀.

Nothing changes with time: each picture is the equilibrium state at the current ε and T.

See itSet ε = 10 meV and warm the bath to 300 K. Watch for: bars on every rung up to n = 9, and the dot on the C/kB chart close to the dashed line at 1.

03

The ladder in a heat bath

The bars are not one system jiggling. They show how a large ensemble of identical modes is spread over the rungs when it is in equilibrium with a bath at temperature T. One sum over the whole ladder, and its derivatives, give everything the sim shows:

Z is the partition function, β = 1/kBT. The sum runs over every rung, not just the ten drawn.
The rung populations. P₀ is the sim's P₀ readout.
  • x compares the gap with the thermal energy. Each step up the ladder multiplies the population by e−x.
  • θ = ε/kB is the spacing written as a temperature, 11.60 K for each meV. For ε = 10 meV, θ = 116.0 K.
  • At T = θ, kBT = ε. Each rung then holds 1/e ≈ 0.37 of the one below, and P₀ = 0.632.
See itSet the temperature to θ, so that kBT = ε. Watch for: kBT equal to ε in the card, and P₀ reading 0.632.
04

Why a cold mode stops absorbing heat

Heat capacity is the energy the mode takes in per kelvin of warming, C = d⟨E⟩/dT. Energy goes in only by lifting systems up the ladder.

When kBT is much smaller than ε (x ≫ 1), almost every system is on the ground rung. A small rise in T lifts only the few in the Boltzmann tail, a fraction e−x of the ensemble, so the mode takes in almost nothing. It is frozen out: the rungs are still there, but the budget cannot pay for the first one.

At T = θ/10 (x = 10) this gives 0.00454, and so does the exact expression.

The fall is exponential in x, not a power of T. That is why the C/kB curve sits near zero and then climbs steeply.

The same mode, ε = 10 meV, at three temperatures: θ/10, 40 K and 1500 K.
See itCool the mode to T = θ/10, keeping your ε (held at 5 meV or more so that θ/10 stays on the slider). Watch for: C/kB dropping below 0.01 while P₀ climbs to 1.
05

The plateau and the half-step

Differentiating ⟨E⟩ gives the whole curve in one variable:

ε T

These sliders move the sim too. T is on a log scale, 5–1500 K.

  • The plateau is kB per mode: ½kB from kinetic and ½kB from potential energy. Dulong–Petit's 3R per mole counts three such modes for each atom.
  • The half-step, C = ½kB, is at x = 2.983, so T½ = 0.3352 θ. For ε = 10 meV that is 38.9 K, the amber marker on the C chart.
  • The approach is quick. C/kB = 0.92 at T = θ and 0.999 at T = 10θ.
  • ⟨E⟩ approaches kBT − ε/2, not kBT, because the lowest rung is at E = 0.
See itPark T on the half-step for your ε. Watch for: C/kB reading 0.500, with the dot on the amber half-step marker.
See itWarm the mode to ten times θ (ε capped at 12 meV so that 10θ fits on the slider). Watch for: the C/kB dot resting on the dashed line at 1.
06

What changing ε does

C/kB depends on T and ε only through x = θ/T, so doubling both leaves it unchanged:

  • The step slides; its shape and height stay. Doubling ε doubles θ, and the whole curve moves to twice the temperature. The plateau is still kB. The half-step goes from 38.9 K to 77.8 K.
  • ⟨E⟩ scales differently. It is ε times a function of x, so doubling T and ε doubles ⟨E⟩. At T = θ it is 5.82 meV for ε = 10 meV and 11.64 meV for ε = 20 meV.
C/kB for ε = 10 and 20 meV on the sim's axes. The curves have the same shape.
See itFrom the half-step at ε = 10 meV, double ε and T together. Watch for: C/kB reading the same before and after, while the half-step marker moves to twice the temperature.
07

Where it matters

One curve serves every ladder. The dots mark where T = 300 K falls for four of them.
  • Many simple solids hold about 3R ≈ 24.9 J mol−1 K−1 at room temperature (Dulong–Petit, 1819): three modes per atom, each on its kB plateau.
  • Diamond has stiff bonds, so ε is large. An Einstein fit gives θE ≈ 1320 K (ε ≈ 114 meV), and C/kB ≈ 0.24 per mode at 300 K, about a quarter of the classical value.
  • Hydrogen gas. The H2 bond vibration has θ ≈ 6330 K, so at 300 K it is frozen out and CV ≈ 5/2 R, not 7/2 R.

This sim models one mode. Real solids and molecules combine many.

Go deeper: where one ladder stops being enough
  • Low T in solids. Real solids follow C ∝ T³ because their lowest-frequency modes have arbitrarily small ε. One fixed ladder falls off exponentially instead. Debye's model repairs this.
  • One ε is a stand-in for diamond. Its vibrations form a band that reaches about 165 meV, where the same formula gives C/kB ≈ 0.07 at 300 K, against 0.24 for the fitted 114 meV.
  • Zero-point energy. With levels at (n + ½)ε, ⟨E⟩ rises by ε/2 and C does not change.
08

Summary

In one line. A mode can absorb heat only if kBT can pay for a rung, so its heat capacity depends on T/θ alone: near zero when kBT ≪ ε, and kB when kBT ≫ ε.

Key points

  • Rung populations fall as e−nx, with x = θ/T.
  • C/kB = x²ex/(ex − 1)²: about x²e−x for x ≫ 1, 1 for x ≪ 1, and ½ at T = 0.3352 θ.
  • ε sets where the step stands, not its height or shape.
  • One mode plateaus at kB. A solid's 3kB per atom is three modes.

Common mix-ups

  • "Heat capacity is a fixed property of a material." The same ladder gives C/kB = 0.005 at θ/10 and 0.999 at 10θ.
  • "A frozen-out mode has gone away." The rungs are still there. Warm the bath and the full kB returns.
  • "The plateau is 3kB." That is per atom, which has three modes. One mode plateaus at kB.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict T½ for ε = 25 meV, then find where C/kB reads 0.500 and compare.
  • At ε = 10 meV, raise T until P₀ reads 0.632 and compare that T with θ.
  • Set ε = 40 meV and T = 300 K and read C/kB. Then work out which ε would put the half-step at 300 K, and whether the slider reaches it.
